tagline: Where elephants and hippos walk the beach
overview:
Gabon straddles the equator on the Atlantic coast of Central Africa, bordered by Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon, and the Republic of the Congo. It is about the size of Colorado, and rainforest covers close to 90 percent of it, one of the highest proportions of any country in the world. The capital, Libreville, is a seaside city of modern towers and palm-lined boulevards whose name means free town, given because it was founded for freed slaves.

Only about 2.4 million people live in Gabon, most of them in Libreville and the oil port of Port-Gentil, so vast stretches of the country are empty of people and full of animals. French is the official language, and Fang, Myene, and other Bantu languages are spoken at home. Oil, manganese, and timber have made Gabon one of the wealthier countries in Africa by average income, though many people remain poor. One family held the presidency for 56 years until the army removed the president in 2023. Gabon has set aside about a tenth of its land as national parks and is a world leader in protecting rainforest.
landAndNature: A narrow coastal plain of lagoons, mangroves, and empty beaches gives way to low mountains and plateaus covered in dense forest, drained by the mighty Ogooué River, which cuts the country in two and carries logs and canoes to the sea. Loango National Park is famous for elephants, buffalo, and hippos that wander onto the beach and even into the surf, while humpback whales breed offshore. Ivindo National Park hides the roaring Kongou Falls and a forest clearing, Langoué Bai, where gorillas and elephants gather. Gabon holds about half of Africa's forest elephants and tens of thousands of gorillas and chimpanzees, plus mandrills, the world's most colorful monkeys, which travel in troops of hundreds. Rain falls heavily most of the year, and the climate is hot and humid.
peopleAndCulture: The Fang are the largest people, along with the Myene, Punu, Nzebi, and Teke, and small communities of Baka forest dwellers. Most Gabonese are Christian, but the Bwiti tradition, with night-long ceremonies of harp music, dance, and a root called iboga, is followed by many and recognized as part of national culture. Meals feature cassava, plantains, and rice with fish, smoked meat, or nyembwe, chicken in a rich palm-nut sauce. Gabonese masks, especially the white-faced Punu masks, are among the most admired African art in the world's museums. Music mixes traditional harps and drums with modern styles, and soccer is the top sport; Gabon hosted the Africa Cup of Nations in 2012 and 2017. Libreville's markets overflow with fabrics, fruit, and seafood.
history: Bantu-speaking peoples moved into the forests over the past 2,000 years, and the Fang arrived from the north in the 1700s and 1800s. Portuguese sailors reached the coast in the 1470s, and for three centuries European ships traded for enslaved people, ivory, and hardwoods. France signed treaties with coastal chiefs in 1839, founded Libreville in 1849 for Africans freed from a captured slave ship, and made Gabon part of French Equatorial Africa. The explorer and doctor Albert Schweitzer built a famous hospital at Lambaréné in 1913. Gabon became independent on August 17, 1960. Omar Bongo took power in 1967 and ruled for 42 years, followed by his son Ali Bongo, until military officers seized power in August 2023, promising elections.
funFacts: At Loango National Park, elephants, buffalo, and hippos can be seen strolling along the beach beside the Atlantic surf.
Gabon is home to about 95,000 forest elephants, more than half of all that remain in Africa.
Libreville means free town in French; it was founded in 1849 for Africans freed from a slave ship.
Mandrills, with their blue and red faces, live in Gabon in troops that can number more than 800 animals.
Rainforest covers almost 90 percent of Gabon, and the country has pledged to keep it standing.
